lede: I use AI every day and I do not trust it by default. Everything here runs with a limit, a test or a human check around the model, because that is the part most AI projects skip.
rules: Anything that can be decided by plain code is decided by plain code. The model only gets a vote on what is left.
Cost, rate and risk limits are enforced outside the model, where a clever prompt cannot talk its way past them.
The model answers in one fixed format. A reply in any other shape is thrown away, never guessed at.
The AI client is replaced in tests, so parsing, refusal and fallback paths are proven offline, with no key and no network.
Benchmarks and logs, not vibes. Negative results get written down too.
Agents do the repeatable work. I set the bar, review the output and carry the blame.

projects.title: AI inside a free product for kids
projects.what: A capped AI helper in Versed Study and AI-built flashcard decks in Versed Learn, in tools used by students.
projects.guard: Per-visitor and per-day limits enforced in a Durable Object after I proved a KV counter could not hold a rate limit. Deck generation is costed at about 3 cents a deck, so the free tier has a real number behind it. No user photo uploads on public content, and chat runs through a word filter with reports.
projects.proof: Write-up: the rate limit that did not limit

projects.title: AI marking for a selection exam
projects.what: An AI-assisted marking platform for a cybersecurity bootcamp's selection exam, built on Claude Sonnet 4 and used on several hundred scripts, past papers and live applicants.
projects.guard: I did not trust it until I had measured it: benchmarked against instructor marking, it agreed about 77% of the time. That number is the point. It tells you the model is a fast first marker, not a judge, and that the disagreements are where a person needs to look.

projects.title: Open-source tools for AI security
projects.what: Three small tools that came out of my own AI work: regression tests for prompt-injection defences, a bit-level audit of a model file against its claimed base, and a probe that tells you whether a model really calls tools.
projects.guard: All three grade with facts, not opinions: a random token either came back or it did not, a bit either changed or it did not. None of them needs a second model to judge the first. Each states its limits in the README, including the case the model audit cannot see.
projects.proof: Code and passing tests on GitHub

projects.title: An LLM in a security pipeline
projects.what: Syslog triage where detection rules and threat-intel matches run first and a language model classifies only what the rules could not settle.
projects.guard: Temperature zero, one fixed answer format, off-format replies discarded. If the API is down the run falls back to the rule results instead of failing. 36 offline tests with the model client faked.
projects.proof: Code and passing tests on GitHub

projects.title: Running large models on my own hardware
projects.what: A 35-billion-parameter model served locally to a chat interface and an agent workspace, on nine-year-old GPUs that current toolkits have dropped.
projects.guard: 46 to 71 tokens a second from measured changes only. A 48K context passed every normal check and then crashed mid-generation, so I now ship only configurations that finish a run at full depth. A script frees GPU memory when a game starts.
projects.proof: Write-up: the benchmarks, including what made it worse

projects.title: A national CTF with AI as a teammate
projects.what: TISC is Singapore's yearly individual capture-the-flag, ten levels that get harder as you go. The 2026 rules allowed AI tools, on the condition that you can explain everything they did. I only started on the final day, and cleared four levels before it closed.
projects.guard: Several challenges planted fake answers addressed to AI agents, so everything a challenge said was treated as untrusted input and none of the decoys were submitted. I kept a notes file per level in my own words, because a step I cannot explain is a step I do not understand yet.

projects.title: Debugging an agent that talked instead of acting
projects.what: My local AI agent kept announcing which tools it would use and then did nothing.
projects.guard: I tested all seven models against a raw tool-call request on both API paths before touching anything. Every model passed, so the model was not the problem. The causes were two layers up: a hidden text-based tool-calling mode, and tool definitions silently cut off by a context-size mismatch.
projects.proof: Write-up: test the layers before theorising

projects.title: An LLM as a bounded decision-maker
projects.what: An opening-range-breakout strategy where code filters the setups and a language model gives the final yes or no.
projects.guard: Drawdown, daily loss and position limits are enforced in code whatever the model says. One trade a day. A cooldown stops repeat calls unless the market has materially moved, which also cut the API bill. Every decision is logged and reviewed twice a week by a separate analysis run.

projects.title: Agents doing real weekly work
projects.what: A scheduled agent pipeline that researches, drafts and builds a week of educational content for Versed, then publishes a review page.
projects.guard: Repeatable steps are scripts run by a cheap model. The expensive model is used once, for writing. Every research citation is verified against a literature database before a deck can ship. Hard rules: no invented users, numbers or quotes.

projects.title: Building with AI coding agents
projects.where: How this site and Versed get made
projects.what: I direct AI coding agents the way I would run a small team: written specs, persistent project notes, review, and tests that have to pass in public.
projects.guard: Nothing ships on the agent's say-so. Claims on this site were checked against the real repositories, which is how five stale tests and one detector that did not do what its README said got found and fixed.
